00013| 
00014| Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering in a single route. At build time, Next.js generates a static HTML shell and a `postponedState` blob for each PPR-enabled route. At request time, the shell is served immediately and dynamic portions are rendered and streamed to the client.
00015| 
00016| This page explains how platforms can implement PPR support at different levels of sophistication.
00017| 
00018| ## How PPR Works
00019| 
00020| ### Build time
00021| 
00022| For each PPR route, Next.js produces:
00023| 
00024| - A **static HTML shell** containing all the content that can be prerendered, with [Suspense](/docs/app/guides/streaming#what-is-streaming) fallbacks where dynamic content will appear.
00025| - A **`postponedState`** value: a serialized string. Treat it as opaque: pass it through without parsing or modifying it. Altering `postponedState` produces incorrect dynamic rendering output.
00026| - An **RSC payload** for the static portions of the page.
00027| 
00028| ### Request time
00029| 
00030| When a request arrives for a PPR route:
00031| 
00032| 1. The server sends the static HTML shell to the client immediately.
00033| 2. The server resumes rendering the dynamic portions using the postponed state.
00034| 3. Dynamic content is streamed to the client, allowing React to hydrate the deferred Suspense boundaries.
00035| 
00036| The client sees the static shell instantly, then dynamic content appears as it resolves.
00037| 
00038| ## Storing PPR Artifacts
00039| 
00040| Each PPR route requires two artifacts to be stored together:
00041| 
00042| 1. The static HTML shell.
00043| 2. The `postponedState` blob.
00044| 
00045| These must be stored and updated atomically. When a PPR route is revalidated (via [time-based](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) or [on-demand revalidation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag)), Next.js regenerates both the shell and the postponed state together. Serving a new shell with an old postponed state, or vice versa, will produce incorrect dynamic content.
00046| 
00047| Use [`requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2`](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter) in your adapter to observe cache updates and propagate them to your storage backend.
00048| 
00049| ## Origin-Only Implementation
00050| 
00051| **This is the simplest approach and works on every platform that supports streaming HTTP responses.**
00052| 
00053| All requests go directly to the Next.js server. The server reads the shell from its local cache, sends it, then renders and streams the dynamic content. This is what `next start` does by default.
00054| 
00055| No additional infrastructure is needed. If your platform supports streaming HTTP responses, it supports PPR.
00056| 
00057| ## CDN Shell + Origin Compute
00058| 
00059| For better TTFB, the static HTML shell can be cached at the CDN edge. When a request arrives:
00060| 
00061| 1. The CDN serves the cached shell immediately (edge latency).
00062| 2. The CDN sends a resume request to the origin server (ideally in parallel with streaming the shell).
00063| 3. The origin server renders only the dynamic portions and streams them back.
00064| 4. The CDN concatenates the shell and dynamic content into a single streaming response to the client.
00065| 
00066| This requires the CDN to support a mechanism for combining cached and dynamic content in a single streaming response. The static shell TTFB drops to edge latency while dynamic content still streams from origin.
00067| 
00068| For the lowest possible latency, the shell can be served from edge storage (for example, a KV store populated during `onBuildComplete`) rather than from a CDN cache. This is a platform architecture decision and does not require any changes to the Next.js application.
00069| 
00070| ## The Resume Protocol
00071| 
00072| The **resume protocol** tells the Next.js handler to skip the shell and render only the dynamic portions. It is used by CDN-to-origin architectures and adapter-based deployments that serve the shell separately.
00073| 
00074| In standard `next start`, the server handles both the shell and dynamic render in a single pass automatically.
00075| 
00076| ### CDN-to-origin
00077| 
00078| When the CDN makes an HTTP request to a separate Next.js origin:
00079| 
00080| - Send a **POST** request to the route with the header `next-resume: 1`.
00081| - Include the `postponedState` blob as the **request body**.
00082| - The server will render only the deferred Suspense boundaries and stream the result.
00083| 
00084| > **Good to know:** When a POST request combines a Server Action with a PPR resume, the request body contains the postponed state followed by the action body. The `x-next-resume-state-length` header carries the byte length of the postponed state prefix so the handler can separate the two. For a pure PPR resume (the common case), the entire request body is the postponed state and this header is not needed.
00085| 
00086| ### Adapter-based
00087| 
00088| When the platform invokes the handler function directly:
00089| 
00090| - Call the entrypoint handler with `req.method` set to `'POST'`, the `next-resume: 1` header on the request, and the `postponedState` as the request body. (You can also pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` as the third argument to the handler invocation, which is equivalent but bypasses the HTTP layer entirely.)
00091| - The handler renders only the deferred Suspense boundaries and streams the result to `res`.
00092| - No HTTP round-trip is needed: the handler is invoked in-process.
00093| 
00094| ### Finding PPR routes in build output
00095| 
00096| In the [adapter output](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/output-types), PPR routes are identified by `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'` in the prerenders array. Iterate `outputs.prerenders` to find these entries and read `fallback.postponedState`.
00097| 
00098| `pprChain.headers` contains the headers needed for the resume protocol: `{ 'next-resume': '1' }`.
00099| 
00100| For detailed implementation with code examples, see [Implementing PPR in an Adapter](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter).
00101| 
00102| ## Implementation Checklist
00103| 
00104| 1. **Read PPR outputs at build time.** In your adapter's `onBuildComplete`, identify prerenders with `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'`. Store the shell HTML and `postponedState` in your cache.
00105| 
00106| 2. **Serve the shell at request time.** For incoming requests to PPR routes, serve the cached shell immediately and begin streaming.
00107| 
00108| 3. **Resume dynamic rendering.** For CDN-to-origin: send a POST request to the Next.js handler with the `next-resume: 1` header and the postponed state as the body. For adapter-based: call the handler directly with POST method and the postponed state in the request body (or pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` to the handler). Stream the response back to the client.
00109| 
00110| 4. **Handle cache updates.** Use `requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2` to capture new shell + postponed state pairs after revalidation, and update your cache atomically.
00111| 
00112| 5. **Support graceful degradation.** If the postponed state is unavailable or stale, fall back to a full server render. The user gets a complete page without the shell-first optimization.
00113| 
00114| For the complete adapter API reference and implementation examples, see the [Deployment Adapter API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/adapterPath).

When [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled, route segment configs like `dynamic`, `revalidate`, and `fetchCache` are replaced by [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) and [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife).

The migration is driven by **instant navigation validation**. With Cache Components enabled, Next.js validates in development whether navigating into each route renders instantly, and surfaces the code that would block it as an error or insight.
